coredata.dc:description:
The ability to (co)polymerize acrylates, methacrylates and styrene with one alkoxyamine/nitroxide has been regarded as challenging in nitroxide mediated polymerization (NMP). The alkoxyamine 3-(((2-cyanopropan-2-yl)oxy)(cyclohexyl)amino)-2,2-dimethyl-3-phenylpropanenitrile (Dispolreg 007) has recently emerged as a robust regulator to mediate the (co)polymerization of methacrylates and styrene. Herein, the versatility of the alkoxyamine is tested to produce random and block copolymers based on n-butyl acrylate (BA). The formation and influence of dead polymer (mostly macromonomers) was studied for the homopolymerziation of n-butyl acrylate. At temperatures above 100 °C, control over the polymerization could be retained up to about 50% conversion, with relatively narrow molar mass distributions ( M
n = 34000 g·mol−1, Ð ∼ 1.7). Above this conversion side reactions, namely β-scission of mid-chain radicals generated by chain transfer to polymer and monomer self-initiation led to loss of control. This effect could be mitigated by lowering to 50 wt% the concentration of BA and/or by lowering the temperature, or by copolymerizing BA with MMA or styrene. The chain extension of acrylate based macro-alkoxyamines led to non linear structures, due to the presence of macromonomers and residual dead chains during the production of PBA macro-alkoxyamines.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para:
The ability to (co)polymerize acrylates, methacrylates and styrene with one alkoxyamine/nitroxide has been regarded as challenging in nitroxide mediated polymerization (NMP). The alkoxyamine 3-(((2-cyanopropan-2-yl)oxy)(cyclohexyl)amino)-2,2-dimethyl-3-phenylpropanenitrile (Dispolreg 007) has recently emerged as a robust regulator to mediate the (co)polymerization of methacrylates and styrene. Herein, the versatility of the alkoxyamine is tested to produce random and block copolymers based on n-butyl acrylate (BA). The formation and influence of dead polymer (mostly macromonomers) was studied for the homopolymerziation of n-butyl acrylate. At temperatures above 100 °C, control over the polymerization could be retained up to about 50% conversion, with relatively narrow molar mass distributions ( M
n = 34000 g·mol−1, Ð ∼ 1.7). Above this conversion side reactions, namely β-scission of mid-chain radicals generated by chain transfer to polymer and monomer self-initiation led to loss of control. This effect could be mitigated by lowering to 50 wt% the concentration of BA and/or by lowering the temperature, or by copolymerizing BA with MMA or styrene. The chain extension of acrylate based macro-alkoxyamines led to non linear structures, due to the presence of macromonomers and residual dead chains during the production of PBA macro-alkoxyamines.

ce:section.ce:para: Reversible deactivation radical polymerization (RDRP) techniques allow for the design of well-defined polymers with predictable molar masses, narrow molar mass distributions and most importantly, block copolymers. Among other tools, transition-metal mediated RDRP (ATRP and derivatives) [1,2], reversible addition fragmentation chain transfer (RAFT) polymerization [3] and nitroxide-mediated polymerization (NMP) [4] have been extensively utilised to design materials with tailored architectures and reactivity. In NMP, the polymerization is mediated by the reversible coupling of a persistent radical (a nitroxide) to a propagating radical, which allows for the reversible formation of dormant and active polymer chains [5]. The balance between dormant/active species is regulated by K , defined as the ratio between the rate constants of dissociation (k D) and of combination (k C) of the two radical species. These rate constants dictate the degree of control over the polymerization and are dependent on the reactivity of the propagating radical, the nature of the nitroxide and polymerization conditions (e.g. temperature, solvent, continuous or semi continuous process) [6,7].

Several monomers can be polymerized by NMP, namely styrene, acrylates and methacrylates [4]. However, the choice of regulator is of upmost importance to mediate the polymerization of said monomers and this is summarized in Table 1 . For instance, TEMPO, TIPNO (2,2,5-trimethyl-4-phenyl-3-azahexane-3-oxyl) and BlocBuilder/SG1 (N-tert-butyl-N-(1-diethylphosphono-2,2-dimethylpropyl)-N-oxyl) can regulate the polymerization of acrylates and styrene but cannot polymerize methacrylates with good control [8–10]. In the case of BlocBuilder, this is ascribed to a strong penultimate effect which undesirably affects the values of k C and k D [11,12]. However, this can be overcome by the random copolymerization of methyl methacrylate with a slight amount of styrene to modify the value of K
[13]. More complex alkoxyamines structures can be also utilised at higher temperatures (upto 200 °C) for the polymerization of acrylates and styrene, with relatively good control [14]. New nitroxides/alkoxyamines such as DPAIO or N-(1-methyl-(1-(4-nitrophenoxy)carbonyl)ethoxy)-N-(1-methyl-(1-(4-nitrophenoxy)carbonyl)ethyl)benzenamine can homopolymerize methyl methacrylate, although with limited monomer conversion and broad molar mass distributions [15,16]. In addition, limited versatility towards other monomers (e.g. acrylates and styrene) is usually observed with these systems, though further modifications of the alkoxyamine structure were shown to improve control in the case of styrene [17]. This situation has been recently rectified with the development of a new generation of alkoxyamines [18]. Specifically, 3-(((2-cyanopropan-2-yl)oxy)(cyclohexyl)amino)-2,2-dimethyl-3-phenylpropanenitrile (Dispolreg 007) has emerged as a robust mediator for the polymerization of both MMA and styrene, both in solution and in aqueous dispersion [19–22]. Good control over the molar mass distributions and good chain end fidelity are obtained with disproportionation being absent within the time scale of polymerization for MMA.

Apart from optimum control over the homopolymerization of various monomers, the interest of NMP lies in the ability to produce block copolymers [4]. These can be produced from the same monomer families (e.g. styrene – styrene derivatives) or with cross families (e.g. styrene – acrylates or styrene – methacrylates). The choice of regulators, among other parameters (see below) is crucial to achieve good control over the chain end fidelity and optimum compatibility between monomers [4]. In Table 2 , the alkoxyamine/nitroxide able to achieve block copolymers are listed.

The ability to produce block copolymers depends on several factors. First the structure of the alkoxyamine/nitroxide should promote the control over the polymerization of the monomers (Scheme 1 ). In addition, sufficient “livingness”, i.e the retention of the reactive chain ends is needed. This “livingness” depends on the combination of monomer and alkoxyamine/nitroxide selected to produce the first block and the reaction conditions (temperature, time, bulk, semi-continuous). The concentration of “living” chains can decrease at high conversions due to side reactions such as chain transfer. Finally, the nature of the monomer will influence the re-initiation step to produce a block copolymer. More specifically, a more stable radical should be preferred for a first block with a less stable radical utilised for the second block.

This combination explains, in part, the inability of most of the nitroxides/alkoxyamines to produce all type of block copolymers. For instance, DPAIO is an efficient regulator for the homopolymerization of methacrylate, though the production of block copolymers from poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) such as PMMA-b-PS and PMMA-b-PBA is more difficult [10,15,17]. This is due, in part, to undesired CO-N dissociation with acrylates and styrene [15]. A modified DPAIO structure (structure 4 in Table 1) could overcome this issue for styrene [17]. In the case of TIPNO, block copolymers containing butyl acrylate and styrene could only be prepared if the poly(butyl acrylate) (PBA) was prepared first [9]. This result was not intuitive, as in terms of radical stability styrene is more stable than butyl acrylate, hence the preparation of PS-b-PBA block copolymer should have been preferred. Nonetheless, this was not successful without modification of the nitroxide structure, in order to enhance the polarity of the nitroxide fragment and change the value of K
[25]. In Table 2, it becomes clear that too few nitroxides/alkoxyamine are able to re-initiate polymerization from a poly(acrylate) block, while displaying good versatility towards other monomers (i.e. methacrylates, styrene). As such, the ability to produce block copolymers from methacrylates, styrene and acrylates with the same alkoxyamine/nitroxide would be a significant breakthrough.

Dispolreg 007 has shown to be a robust regulator for the homopolymerization of methacrylates and styrene. Block copolymers of PMMA-b-PBMA, PMMA-b-PS and PS-b-PMMA could also be obtained with good control [18,19,22]. In addition, PMMA-b-PBA could also be obtained, although the conversion achieved for the second block was relatively low (40%) [19]. At first sight, this suggests that Dispolreg 007 is able to control the polymerization of acrylates, which will make it as the only alkoxyamine able to control the main families of monomers (i.e. styrene, acrylates and methacrylates).

Therefore, in this work, the extent to which the polymerization of acrylates can be controlled by Dispolreg 007 was investigated. Then, the possibility to synthesize PBA-b-PS block copolymers was explored. As the dissociation energy of the CON bond (calculated utilizing density functional theory) is higher for BA than for MMA and styrene (MMA (142.30 kJ/mol) < S (169.04 kJ/mol) < BA (172.76 kJ/mol)) a temperature at least as high as that used for styrene (126 °C) [22] seems to be needed to achieve good control over the homopolymerization a priori. However, at this temperature significant effects of thermal initiation, backbiting and β-scission are to be expected [28–30]. Therefore, the effect of temperature was investigated first in the homopolymerization of BA, in an attempt to find a region where K is high enough and backbiting and β-scission are acceptable. The retention of the alkoxyamine chain ends was tested by chain extension with styrene to yield PBA-b-PS block copolymers. A deeper insight on the chain end fidelity was achieved through the preparation of a macroalkoxyamine containing fluorescein o-acrylate (FA) and BA, subsequently chain extended with styrene. BA was also copolymerized in the presence of various amounts (ranging from 5 wt% to 80 wt%) of co-monomer (styrene or MMA) in an attempt to mitigate the influence of side reactions.

Styrene (Quimidroga, technical grade), methyl methacrylate (MMA, Quimidroga, technical grade), n-butyl acrylate (BA, Quimidroga, technical grade) were distilled under reduced pressure and stored at 5 °C before use. Toluene (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich), tert-butylbenzene (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich), HPLC grade tetrahydrofuran (THF, Scharlab) and Fluorescein o-acrylate (95%, Sigma-Aldrich) were used as received. The alkoxyamine Dispolreg 007 was synthesized according to the reported procedure [18].
1H and 13C NMR spectra were recorded on a Bruker DPX-400 spectrometer using deuterated solvents obtained from Sigma-Aldrich.

SEC traces were obtained on a set up consisting of a pump (LC-20A, Shimadzu), an autosampler (Waters 717), a differential refractometer (Waters 2410) a UV-detector (Waters 2410), a fluorescence detector (Waters FLR 2475) and three columns in series (Styragel HR2, HR4 and HR6 with pore sizes ranging from 102 to 106 Å). Chromatograms were obtained in THF (HPLC grade) at 35 °C using a flow rate of 1 mL·min−1. The equipment was calibrated using narrow polystyrene standards (K = 11.4·10−5 dL·g−1, α = 0.716) [31] ranging from 595 to 3.95 × 106 Da (5th order universal calibration). The resulting molar mass distributions have been recalibrated using the Mark-Houwink parameters for poly(n-butyl acrylate) (K = 12.2·10−5 dL·g−1, α = 0.70) [31]. All samples were passed through 0.45-µm nylon filter before analysis.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Polymerization of n-butyl acrylate in the presence of Dispolreg 007
ce:section.ce:para: In a typical procedure, Dispolreg 007 (265 mg, 0.78 mmol), n-butyl acrylate (30 g, 300 equiv, 75 wt%) and tert-butylbenzene (10 g) were charged into a three-neck 100-mL round-bottom flask (RBF) fitted with a stirring bar, thermometer and rubber seals. The mixture was stirred and deoxygenated with nitrogen for 30 min and subsequently placed in a pre-heated oil bath. The temperature was controlled inside the solution, which was left to polymerize at the desired temperature for at least 5 h. To prevent an exotherm at the onset of polymerization for solids contents at 50 wt% and above, the temperature was carefully monitored and the RBF was temporarily taken out and re-immersed into the oil bath to maintain the targeted polymerization temperature. Samples for conversion and SEC analysis were carefully taken from the polymerization mixture via a deoxygenated syringe. Monomer conversion was calculated from gravimetric analysis. After polymerization the solution was diluted in THF, precipitated in cold MeOH and dried under vacuum to yield a colourless viscous liquid.

A poly(n-butyl acrylate) macro-alkoxyamine (234 mg; target DP n = 100, stopped at 55% conversion, M
n = 9800 g·mol−1, 1 equiv), prepared via the pre-detailed procedure (at 106 °C, 50 wt% in tert-butylbenzene) was added to a 50-mL RBF fitted with a magnetic stirring bar and rubber seals. Styrene (2 g, 19.2 mmol, 800 equiv) and tert-butylbenzene (3 g) were added and the solution was left to stir and deoxygenate with nitrogen for 30 min. Subsequently, the mixture was placed in a pre-heated oil bath and left to polymerize at 126 °C overnight. Then, a sample was isolated for gravimetric analysis, whilst the remaining solution was cooled, diluted in THF, precipitated twice in MeOH and dried under vacuum to yield a white solid. The resulting polymer was analyzed by SEC.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Batch polymerization of n-butyl acrylate in the presence of Dispolreg 007
ce:section.ce:para: First, the influence of temperature on the polymerization of BA in the presence of Dispolreg 007 was studied. Temperatures ranging from 86 °C up to 116 °C were tested, whilst targeting the same degree of polymerization (DP n), [Dispolreg 007]:[BA] = 1:300 at 75 wt% in tert-butylbenzene. The kinetic results are summarized in Fig. 1 .

The increase of temperature induces several changes in the polymerization kinetics, the first of which being an increase of the overall rate of polymerization. The values for conversions achieved for T ≤ 96 °C were too low and hence discussion is focused on the polymerizations carried out at 106 °C and 116 °C. After about 15% conversion, the Ln([M]0/[M]) plots are rather linear (Fig. 1A). The initial rapid polymerization rate is due to the decomposition of the alkoxyamine, which at T ≥ 106 °C is expected to be complete at low conversions. The subsequent decrease of the polymerization rate was due to the strong C-ON bond formed with the butyl acrylate terminal unit in the macro-alkoxyamine. This shifts the equilibrium towards the dormant state, thus decreasing the concentration of radical in the system [32,33].

Fig. 1B shows that the evolution of molar mass with conversion deviates from the theoretical values. At low conversions, the molar mass is above the theoretical values, which is believed to be due to the combination of the relatively slow initiation of the alkoxyamine [39] and the high k p of the monomer [34,35] compared to the rate of recombination, thus promoting the incorporation of a large number of monomer units per recombination/decomposition cycle. As conversion increases, the molar masses are closer to the theoretical values, while at higher conversion (>50%), the measured molar masses are below the theoretical line, which strongly indicates the formation of new chains.

Fig. 2 shows that there is quite a good control of the molar masses up to about 50% conversion, although the relatively stable low molar mass tail indicates the continuous formation of new short chains. At higher conversions, a high molar mass shoulder appears, resulting in a strong increase in the dispersity values (Fig. 1C).

The results can be analyzed using Scheme 1, which summarizes the most likely mechanisms. According to this scheme, small radicals – responsible for the stable low molar mass tail – can be produced by thermal initiation of the monomer and by β-scission of mid-chain radicals formed by backbiting [36,37]. Delayed dissociation of the alkoxyamine could not be of fault, as discussed above, due to an expected full decomposition of the alkoxyamine at low conversions at T ≥ 106 °C [18].

The existence of backbiting is supported by NMR of the last sample of the polymerization carried out at 116 °C (Fig. S1), which shows the presence of vinyl bonds (from the macromonomers) in the 1H NMR and quaternary carbons (from branch points) in the 13C NMR spectra. The branching fraction ( C
q) can be extracted from the 13C NMR, by comparison of the polymer terminal
C H3 (δ = 11–14 ppm) and quaternary carbons (δ = 45–49 ppm, resulting from the formation of long- and short-chain branches). This yields 1.2% of branching, in line with previous investigations [38].

A way to check the relative importance of the radical generation by thermal initiation is to vary monomer concentration. As thermal initiation is a second order process [39], a decrease of the concentration of BA should lower the influence of this mechanism. In addition, a lower monomer content should increase the propensity for consecutive backbiting and β-scission. The results of batch solution polymerization of BA ([Dispolreg 007]:[BA] = 1:300; 116 °C) with monomer contents ranging from 20 wt% to 75 wt% in tert-butylbenzene are summarized in Fig. 3 .

The decrease of monomer content lowers the radical concentration (proportional to the slope of the Ln([M]0/[M]) versus time plot) due to the decrease in alkoxyamine concentration and supposedly the impact of radical generation by thermal initiation [18,22]. However, comparing the values of the slopes (0.66 × 10−2, 0.51 × 10−2 and 0.26 × 10−2 min−1 for 75, 50 and 20 wt% of BA, respectively) does not allow any conclusion to be drawn, as more bimolecular termination (second order process) is expected for higher monomer (and alkoxyamine) concentrations. On the other hand, the evolution of the molar masses is more conclusive. Fig. 3B shows that the decrease of monomer content from 75 wt% to 50 wt% appears to enhance the control over the polymerization of BA in the presence of Dispolreg 007, as the discrepancy between expected and measured molar masses is reduced. In addition, the dispersity values are lower, going from Ð ∼ 5 to Ð ∼ 3. Furthermore, the molar mass distributions show a clear shift of the low molar mass tail to higher values during polymerization, which supports the relevance of radicals formed by thermal initiation (Fig. 4 ). The significance of thermal initiation to the contribution of radicals was further checked by performing a thermally initiated polymerization of BA under similar reaction conditions (116 °C, 75 wt% solids in tert-butylbenzene). Fig. S2 shows that a monomer conversion of around 20% was achieved within 6 h. In addition, M n was about 200,000 g/mol, which is in good agreement with the shoulder of the molar mass distribution in Fig. 2 (bottom).

Further reduction of the BA concentration to 20 wt% solids led to almost constant molar masses and dispersity values (Ð ∼ 1.7–1.8). The most likely reason is that the low monomer concentration led to such a strong increase in the rates of both backbiting and β-scission relative to propagation that this controlled the molar masses. The importance of these reactions is confirmed by 1H NMR (Fig. 5 ), through the comparison of the H
2CC shifts from the macromonomer (δ = 5.5–6.5 ppm) and the OC H
2 of the PBA and macromonomer (δ = 4.1 ppm). It was estimated that 65% ( = 100 × ( H
2CC/OC H
2) × DP n) of the chains were generated from β-scission. This value is almost double of what was observed when the solid content was 75 wt% (33% of the chains, Fig. S1).

Above 50 wt% of monomer, the molar mass distributions show the formation of a high molar mass shoulder at conversions higher than 50% (Figs. 2 and 4, bottom). It may be argued that this is the result of the incorporation of macromonomers to the growing chains [40]. However, the fact that the molar mass of the shoulder is about one order of magnitude higher than that of the main peak does not support this hypothesis, as this would require the incorporation of an average of ten macromonomers per chain. The unlikelihood of the massive incorporation of macromonomers is supported by the absence of a high molar mass shoulder in the experiment carried out at 20 wt% of BA (Fig. 4, top), in which the concentration of macromonomers was maximal. Thus, although the possible reincorporation of macromonomer cannot be excluded, this is not the reason behind the appearance of the high molar mass shoulder. Another possibility is the lack of control in the second part of the process (for conversion higher than 50%). This was examined by using a mathematical model (Supporting Information). Although there is uncertainty about the values of some of the parameters of the model (Table S2), the simulations clearly show that the reason for the lack of control in the second part of the polymerization is that the concentration of nitroxide decreased to a very low value, which is assumed to be due to the reaction with radicals generated by thermal initiation. The low concentration of nitroxide results in huge amount of monomer units being added per activation/deactivation cycle, leading to loss of control (Fig. S3). It should be noted that in addition to thermal initiation, alternative reactions that result in consumption of the nitroxide, such as radical transfer, radical addition and decomposition [41–43], would also result in a similar outcome and cannot be ruled out.

This observation is in sharp contrast with previous investigation on the polymerization of BA using SG1/BlocBuilder, TIPNO or more complex nitroxides [8,9,14,44,45]. As a result of the low concentration of nitroxide and the unfavourable rate constants, side reactions become predominant above 50% conversion herein, which is not the case when the abovementioned regulators are utilised.

According to the model, β-scission of mid-chain radicals generated by backbiting play a leading role in the decrease of M
n. The model also showed that the majority of “dead” chains are macromonomers, in agreement with the macromonomer content as measured by 1H NMR (Fig. 5).

It may be thought that the addition of an excess of nitroxide at the onset of the reaction would improve the control of the polymerization of BA with Dispolreg 007 [8,9,46]. Due to difficulties in the isolation of the nitroxide part of Dispolreg 007, we tested this idea by addition of a small excess (5 mol %) of SG1 to the reaction. In Fig. S4, it can be seen that the control of the polymerization of BA ([BA]:[Dispolreg 007]:[SG1] = 100:1:0.05, at 106 °C, 50 wt% solids in tert-butylbenzene) is improved, although high dispersity values are still observed (Ð ∼ 3).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Chain extension of poly(n-butyl acrylate) based macro-alkoxyamine with styrene
ce:section.ce:para: In the discussion above, it has been suggested that for conversions below 50%, the strong CON bond of the macro-alkoxyamine would favor the dormant side of the polymerization. Hence, the retention of alkoxyamine chain ends should be high, which would allow for the synthesis of a block copolymer upon addition of a second monomer. On the other hand, at higher conversions the polymer was a mixture of macro-alkoxyamines and macromonomer, which reduces the potential for the production of block copolymers. However, incorporation of the poly(n-butyl acrylate) macromonomer species into “living” chains by reaction with the propagating radical is also possible, which may limit the impact of β-scission reactions on the ability to form copolymers, although it lowers the amount of well-defined block copolymers.

Consequently, we sought to check these hypotheses by investigating the chain extension of PBA based macro-alkoxyamines obtained at different BA conversions. Two macro-alkoxyamines were prepared in batch at 96 °C and three at 106 °C ([Dispolreg 007]:[BA] = 1:100, 75 wt% in tert-butylbenzene).

For similar BA conversions a lower fraction of macromonomers is expected at 96 °C. At this temperature the polymerizations were stopped at 55% and 70% monomer conversion (Table S1, lines 1 and 2). After purification the macro-alkoxyamines were reacted in the presence of styrene and the polymerization analyzed by SEC. Fig. 6 shows that in agreement with the assumption of a weaker β-scission, a high molar mass shoulder in the PBA only appears for the 70% conversion experiment.

When the macro-alkoxyamine was stopped at 55% monomer conversion, good chain extension was observed with styrene, thus yielding a PBA-b-PS block copolymer with 65% monomer conversion (Table S1, line 1). A clear shift towards higher molar masses is observed in SEC, while the UV signal overlaps with the signal obtained in the DRI detector, thus confirming the presence of the styrene moieties in most, if not all chains (Fig. S5). After chain extension the dispersity value remains unchanged for the PBA-b-PS copolymer (Ð ∼ 1.67), which suggests a small presence of dead chains.

The macro-alkoxyamine stopped at 70% conversion was also utilized to prepare a PBA-block-PS block copolymer. The dispersity value for the macro-alkoxyamine is higher than in the case of a macro-alkoxyamine stopped at 55% conversion (Ð ∼ 1.95), with a small shoulder visible at high molar mass. The chain extension of PBA with styrene reached 64% monomer conversion (Table S1, line 2), while a shift towards higher molar masses is evident from SEC (Fig. 6). Remarkably, the dispersity value decreases for the copolymer (Ð ∼ 1.58) and the high molecular weight dead PBA chains do not appear as a shoulder in the molar mass distribution of the extended copolymer. It may be argued that the dead PBA is hidden due to the overlap with the extended copolymer in the region 20–27 min (retention time, corresponding to 40,000–300,000 Da), but the good agreement between the UV and DRI detectors in this region (Fig. S5), strongly indicates that a large fraction of the “dead” PBA contained in the shoulder has actually been incorporated into the copolymer. This confirms the hypothesis that this fraction corresponds to the macromonomers formed by β-scission.

A more difficult case is the extension of the macro-alkoxyamines prepared at 106 °C ([Dispolreg 007]:[BA] = 1:100, 75 wt% in tert-butylbenzene) and stopped at 61%, 75% and 83% monomer conversion (Table S1, lines 3, 4 and 5). The macro-alkoxyamines were utilized to initiate polymerization of styrene, achieving 71%, 77% and 78% monomer conversion, respectively (Table S1). Fig. 7 shows the molar mass distributions of the macro-alkoxyamines and the extended copolymers.

It can be seen that in all cases, there is a neat shift towards higher molar masses with a substantial decrease in dispersity values. In addition, the UV traces overlap the refractive index signals and no residual high molar mass shoulders are observed. This demonstrates the presence of styrene in most of the polymer chains and that the population of high molar mass dead chains formed during the preparation of the macro-alkoxyamines is incorporated within the copolymer molar mass distribution. The incorporation of the macromonomers during chain extension is confirmed by 1H NMR (Fig. S6), in which the disappearance of the CC H
2 protons (from the macromonomers, δ = 5.5–6.5 ppm) is clearly visible after the chain extension.

Although the UV–vis detection can give a relatively good insight on the chain extension, it can be argued that the success of the formation of a PBA-b-PS block copolymer is biased by the difference in the dn/dc values between the PBA-macroalkoxyamine (dn/dc = 6.5 × 10−2 mg·L−1, λ0 = 546 nm) and the newly formed PS block (dn/dc = 1.9 × 10−1 mg·L−1, λ0 = 546 nm) [47]. In order to clarify this issue, the success of the chain extension of a PBA-macroalkoxyamine with styrene was monitored by fluorescence. First, a random copolymer of BA with fluorescein o-acrylate (FA) was prepared at 106 °C ([BA]:[FA]:[Dispolreg 007] = 100:5:1, 50 wt% in tert-butylbenzene) and stopped at 70% monomer conversion thus yielding a PBA-co-PFA copolymer with M n = 14000 g·mol−1 and Ð = 1.58 (Fig. S7 and Table S1). Surprisingly, there was no apparent shoulder at high molar masses, due to an unexpectedly lower amount of macromonomers from β-scission (4%). This might be due to the combination of moderate temperature (106 °C) and low solids contents (50 wt%), in line with the discussions above. In Fig. 8 , the small distribution at high retention times correspond to the presence of residual monomer before purification. The purified macroalkoxyamine was utilized to mediate the polymerization of styrene at 126 °C, yielding 90% monomer conversion and M n = 67200 g·mol−1 with relatively broad molar mass distribution (Ð = 2.56, Fig. 8). The presence of the fluorescent monomer gives a deeper insight on the success of the chain extension, with the molar mass distributions shifting to lower retention times (i.e. higher molar masses) in Fig. 8. The presence of a low molar mass tailing after chain extension can be ascribed to the re-incorporation of macromonomers formed during the synthesis of the macroalkoxyamine at 106 °C.

These observations show that Dispolreg 007 allows for the formation of PBA-b-PS block copolymers over a wide range of BA conversions achieved in the first polymerization stage. The formation of PBA-b-PS block copolymers is favored when low temperatures are used in the polymerization of BA and conversion of BA is limited (typically to about 50%). On the other hand, higher temperatures and BA conversions lead to mixtures of PBA-b-PS and PBA-b-P(S-co-PBAmacro) copolymers.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Can the polymerization kinetics be improved through batch copolymerization of n-Butyl acrylate with styrene or methyl methacrylate in the presence of Dispolreg 007?
ce:section.ce:para: A way to further improve the control over the polymerization is by introducing a co-monomer, as proposed by Charleux et al. [13]. In principle, one can optimize the polymerization by selecting a co-monomer with a favorable reactivity ratio with the “main” monomer in addition to optimum rate constants of combination and dissociation.

In the case of BA, the high k p of the monomer results in the incorporation of many monomer units per dissociation/recombination cycle, as k p BA [BA] ≫ k c macro-alkoxyamine [Nitroxide]. However, the addition of a co-monomer with a lower k p can reduce the number of monomer units added per cycle, as long as k p co-monomer/k c co-monomer < k p BA/k c BA. MMA and styrene fulfill this condition, can be homopolymerized with good control with Dispolreg 007 and their corresponding reactivity ratios (see below) favor their presence as the terminal unit compared to that of BA [18,22]. Hence, they are good candidates for the copolymerization approach. First, BA and styrene were copolymerized in the presence of Dispolreg 007 at 115 °C with various contents of styrene ranging from 5 to 80 wt% while targeting similar molar masses ( M
n = 38800 g·mol−1) and with a fixed solids content of 75 wt% in tert-butylbenzene. The kinetic results are summarized in Fig. 9 .

The introduction of styrene as co-monomer in the polymerization of BA in the presence of Dispolreg 007 has a strong influence on the kinetics. Fig. 9A shows that as the content of co-monomer increases, the dominance of styrene in the copolymerization kinetics becomes greater, thus decreasing the overall rate of polymerization due to the low k p of styrene at this temperature [22].

The increasing content of styrene has a positive effect on the control of both molar masses and dispersity value. When the concentration of styrene increases from 5 to 20 wt%, the discrepancy between measured and theoretical molar masses is decreased, though the experimental molar masses are still below the expected values. This is due to the thermal initiation of both monomers, as previously reported [22]. The dispersity values at high conversion are also decreased, from Ð ∼ 5 to Ð ∼ 1.8. At a styrene content of 80 wt%, the measured molar masses are close to theoretical, while the dispersity values are lower, which suggest an improved control. It should be noted that the likelihood of chain transfer reaction of the acrylics (intra and inter-molecular) is reduced as the content of the co-monomer is increased and can be negligible for co-monomer contents above 20 wt%, according to previous investigations [37,48,49].

The weight fraction butyl acrylate in the copolymer was calculated from the NMR spectrum in Fig. 10 , through the comparison of the integrals of the H CCH (δ = 6–7.4 ppm) for the styrene units with the C H
3 (δ = 0.9 ppm) and the C(O)OC H
2 (δ = 3.6 ppm) of the acrylate units. The estimated content of butyl acrylate in a copolymer is 21.2–23.0 wt%, which is close to theoretical calculations (26 wt% with r BA = 0.22–0.26 and r S = 0.68–0.82 at 110 °C) [50].

The tolerance to BA in a copolymerization is also tested utilizing 20 wt% of BA as a co-monomer in MMA polymerization. The reactivity ratios between MMA and BA are r MMA = 2.42 and r BA = 0.46 at 100 °C [51], thus favoring the presence of methyl methacrylate as the end unit. In addition, Dispolreg 007 has been shown to mediate the polymerization MMA with good control.

During the copolymerization, a linear increase of molar mass with conversion can be observed without extensive deviation from expected values. The final dispersity value for the copolymer is Ð ∼ 1.6 which demonstrates a good tolerance to BA in the copolymerization. In Fig. 11 A the livingness of the system can be noticed by the linear increase of Ln([M]0/[M]) with time, which highlights the positive influence of the high content of MMA in the copolymerization kinetics.

The weight fraction of PBA was calculated from the NMR spectrum (Fig. S8), through the comparison of the integrals of the C(O)OC H
3 (δ = 3.6 ppm) of the methacrylate units with the C H
3 (δ = 0.9 ppm) and the C(O)OC H
2 (δ = 3.9 ppm) of the acrylate units. The estimated content of butyl acrylate in the copolymer is 8.0–8.6 wt%, which is close to the theoretical value of 10 wt%, using the reactivity ratios and monomer weight fractions provided above.
These results show that Dispolreg 007 was able to control the copolymerization of BA with styrene and MMA up to high monomer conversions (>80%) when the amount of BA was below 21 wt%.

It has been demonstrated that the alkoxyamine 3-(((2-cyanopropan-2-yl)oxy)(cyclohexyl)amino)-2,2-dimethyl-3-phenylpropanenitrile (Dispolreg 007) allows for the formation of poly(butyl acrylate)-b-poly(styrene) (PBA-b-PS) block copolymers over a wide range of BA conversions achieved in the preparation of the macro-alkoxyamines. The careful preparation of the macro-alkoxyamine was found to be important and was investigated during the homolymerization of BA at 116 °C with solids content of 75 wt%, showing good control up to about 50%, above which the control was lost. Analysis of the experimental results with a mathematical model showed that the lack of control was due to the consumption of nitroxide, resulting in slow recombination of the propagating radical relative to propagation, as well as the presence of secondary reactions such as backbiting and β-scission. The mathematical model showed that the majority of “dead” chains were macromonomers. Reduction of the solids content to 50 wt% improved the control over the polymerization. Further decrease of monomer concentration to 20 wt% led to a dramatic increase of the rates of backbiting and β-scission, thus a loss of control. As such, the formation of well defined PBA-b-PS copolymers was favoured when low temperatures were utilized in the polymerization of BA (96 °C) and when the conversion of BA was limited to about 50%. Higher temperatures and BA conversions led to mixtures of PBA-b-PS and PBA-b-P(S-co-PBAmacro) with no traces of residual PBA chains, which confirmed the full incorporation of the PBA macromonomers in the copolymer. Finally, copolymerization with styrene and methyl methacrylate improved control at high co-monomer fractions. Overall, these results show the good versatility of Dispolreg 007 in its ability to copolymerize acrylates, methacrylates and styrene with relatively good control.
